HTML and text both should default to UTF8 as the default encoding. Encodings fill a somewhat odd role since they are both encodings and formats (with the text format plus a given encoding being the same thing as that encoding by itself).
Most formats have language variant types, for printing structured metadata where it’s not supported. Whether it should be printed by default is debateable.

Language variants aren’t handled as format variants of the languages they are variants of, since there aren’t tons of possible combinations (at least that are practical to support). Instead, the type is given as lv: followed by the language identifier of which they are a variant (without the lang_ prefix).

Programming languages are both formats on their own account, and variants of other formats: for exporting to a text-based format, you could opt to have programmatic Dcs exported to a programming language or a natlang.

column10: Like DcText, but Dcs are short by default. @123@ = short Dc 123; a = literal Unicode a; @l123@ = long Dc 123; @L123@ = local node; @u123a@ = U+123A, @f123@ = format 123

Like DcUtf, but begins with magic DcMM\0, followed by the binary equivalent of UUID d5ab819e-9b8e-4d61-adbc-933e8851e79a, and subsequently, any occurrence of Dc 203 will be followed by a type byte (0 = binary; 1 = DcUtf; 2 and 5..255 reserved), followed by a 128-bit binary number (big-endian) indicating the size of the encapsulated region (even if that size is 0), and then the contents of that region will be stored directly as binary data rather than using base64 encapsulation. The terminating Dc 204 will be implicit. If Dcs other than base64-encapsulation or padding Dcs occur prior to a terminating Dc 204, the region will use normal DcUtf (type byte 1) rather than binary. Type bytes 3 and 4 are the same as 0 and 1, but there is additionally a binary sha256 checksum of the stream following the size.
